title: 2025-06-17 Redwood migration demo: OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood
summary: Demo focused on parity mapping and migration path from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API. Covered request/response parity, streaming, function calling, embeddings differences, costs, latency expectations, VPC/private deployment considerations, and next steps to run a pilot and benchmark. SE did a deep-dive on API mapping and runtime behaviors; AE recapped pricing/contract options and arranged security docs share.
next_steps: Redwood to share migration parity spreadsheet and sample mapping doc - Maya to send (by 2025-06-18)
Customer to provide 3 representative prompts and current token/cost numbers - Laura (by 2025-06-20)
Schedule 1-week pilot run and latency benchmark with dedicated capacity - Maya/Ethan to propose times (by 2025-06-19)
Send SOC 2 and KMS integration docs - Jordan (by 2025-06-18)
action_items: Maya Chen: Send parity spreadsheet + pricing sheet (due 2025-06-18)
Ethan Park: Prepare benchmark run template and example config for Together/Anthropic/OpenAI parity (due 2025-06-19)
Laura Kim: Share 3 sample prompts and current usage logs (due 2025-06-20)
Ben Gomez: Confirm network constraints for VPC/private deployment (due 2025-06-20)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood. We'll kick off with a short agenda, then Ethan will walk through the parity mapping and demo.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Thanks Maya, we have Laura and Ben on, we use OpenAI and Together in prod and Anthropic for few safety-sensitive flows, so main ask is: how close is Redwood to parity and what is the migration effort.
[00:35] Ethan Park: Great question. High level, Redwood API supports the same shape of calls you’re used to - generation, chat, embeddings, and function calling. We'll show a direct mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together params to Redwood equivalents and run a short live example.
[00:50] Laura Kim: Quick note, for embeddings we currently use text-embedding-ada-002 and also a custom fine-tuned approach with Together; cost and dimensional parity matter.
[01:05] Ethan Park: Yep, we'll cover that. Also budget note: Redwood token accounting aligns with standard tokenization but our cost per token differs by model family and quantization; we put the mapping in the spreadsheet we'll share.
[01:22] Ben Gomez: Also need to understand VPC/peering for private deployment, and whether audit logs/KMS integrate with our existing GCP KMS.
[01:36] Jordan Liu: On the private side we have both VPC and on-prem options. We integrate with customer KMS (HSM tooling too), and audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM. We'll send the security packet after.
[01:52] Samir Patel: Cool, thanks.
[02:00] Ethan Park: Ok demo time. I'm going to paste a small OpenAI chat snippet, then show equivalent Redwood request. Note, there might be slight transcription errors as I read off the code.
[02:15] Ethan Park: (shares screen) OpenAI call: model: gpt-4o-mini, messages: [...], temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 512, stream: true, functions: [moderation-check]. Equivalent Redwood request: model: redwood/gpt4o-mini (model alias), temp: 0.2, max_tokens: 512, streaming=true, tool_calls=[moderation_check]. The mapping is 1:1 for parameters, and streaming uses the same SSE style so client-side SDKs just plug in.
[02:45] Laura Kim: When you say streaming same SSE, does that mean we can reuse our existing client code with minimal changes?
[02:53] Ethan Park: Yes, in most cases it's a rename of endpoint and minor SDK init changes. We have SDK adapters and a migration helper that swaps the headers and maps function signatures.
[03:05] Samir Patel: How about Anthropic-to-Redwood? Anthropic has different chat turn formats.
[03:12] Ethan Park: Good point. Anthropic's prompt style is slightly different, but we provide a prompt-translator in the helper script that converts assistant/system/user tokens and mapping for safety settings. You may see small differences in few edge cases; we include eval harness to compare outputs.
[03:28] Ben Gomez: Tokenization differs between models — how do you ensure cost parity?
[03:33] Ethan Park: We run tokenizer snapshots and provide tokenized counts in the spreadsheet. For cost parity we recommend trying Redwood's quantized variants which reduce bytes per token and give similar output quality; our Optimize tool suggests quantization profile by workload.
[03:50] Laura Kim: About embeddings: Together's embeddings are 1536 dims for our workflow, while text-embedding-ada-002 is 1536 as well but we have slight differences in vector distribution. How do we handle downstream vector DB compat?
[04:05] Jordan Liu: You'll get stable dims from Redwood models we surface; there are 1-to-1 drop-in embeddings where we guarantee same dims. If distribution differs we recommend reindexing or running a small A/B compare. We also surface cosine-normalized outputs if you rely on specific DB ops.
[04:22] Maya Chen: I'll drop the parity spreadsheet and a quick migration playbook in the chat after the call, plus links to the security pack.
[04:30] [00:04:30] Aisha Rahman: A quick operational question: what's the rollback story if a new model variant causes quality regression?
[04:38] Ethan Park: Redwood has rollout constructs: canary percent, A/B routing, automatic fallback to previous model and automatic vote-based routing if quality drops. You can pin versions per route so rollbacks are fast.
[04:50] Samir Patel: Great. Also need to validate latency — our SLAs are 300ms p95 for short-turn chat. Can Redwood meet that on hosted?
[04:59] Ethan Park: For short-turn chat we recommend either Redwood Dedicated or local hot-warm pools. Hosted latency can be competitive but dedicated gives guaranteed p95 with reserved capacity. We'll propose a dedicated bench run as part of the pilot.
[05:15] Laura Kim: Any gotchas around function/tool calling? We rely on structured JSON outputs and function arg types.
[05:23] Ethan Park: Function calling in Redwood supports the same schema as OpenAI; we also have JSON schema validation and structured output enforcement. Minor differences: the helper maps ambiguous types and we've seen name collisions in some Anthropic exported function metadata — helper script handles renaming.
[05:40] Ben Gomez: Security: SOC2, SAML, RBAC — do you support enterprise SSO and per-route RBAC?
[05:47] Jordan Liu: Yes, SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, RBAC at route/model level, audit logs retention configurable. We'll share SOC2 report and integration guides.
[05:58] [00:05:58] Laura Kim: Cost question: you mentioned quantized variants - how much cheaper are they compared to hosted OpenAI for embeddings and chat?
[06:07] Maya Chen: It depends on workload and token mix; but typical quantized call can be 30-60% cheaper per token than standard float models. Our Optimize tool suggests batching, prefix caching, and quantization combo to hit cost goals.
[06:22] Ethan Park: I'll show a quick Optimize view in the Console. (switches screen) Here's a sample workload: percent tokens long-tail, batching opportunity, our recommendations show estimated unit cost and expected latency.
[06:38] Samir Patel: Do you have a demo link or a spreadsheet for this?
[06:42] Maya Chen: Yes, link in chat: https://redwood.example.com/migration/parity-spreadsheet and security pack: https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2-kms. We'll email the PDFs as well.
[06:55] [00:06:55] Ethan Park: Live quick test: I'll do a small generation from a Together-like model and compare to Redwood's variant. Expect some small transcript mismatches.
[07:05] Ethan Park: (runs test) Together request: model: together/eleven-light, temp:0.1, max_tokens:128, streaming false. Output: "Hello team, here's the summary..." Redwood equivalent: model: redwood/eleven-light-quant, temp 0.1, max_tokens 128. Output: "Hello team, here's the summary..." Quality is comparable; we run a fuzzy-match eval to quantify MEA and edit-distance.
[07:30] Laura Kim: Nice. Any limits around KV cache behavior for multi-session chat? We rely on large KV cache to avoid re-calc.
[07:38] Ethan Park: Runtime supports KV cache and we expose TTL controls; continuous batching can keep cache warm across sessions if pinned to dedicated pools. There can be small differences in eviction semantics but we include config knobs.
[07:52] Samir Patel: Can we bring our own models into Redwood, e.g., Hugging Face or private together models?
[07:59] Jordan Liu: For Private deployments yes, you can register custom model artifacts. For hosted we support vetted public models; private option lets you bring your own weights.
[08:10] Ben Gomez: For the pilot we'll want to test 3 routes: short chat, long-form generation, and embeddings index refresh.
[08:17] Ethan Park: Perfect. We'll prepare example configs for each.
[08:22] [00:08:22] Aisha Rahman: Timeline question: how long to move from proof-of-concept to pilot?
[08:28] Maya Chen: Typically 2-4 weeks to pilot depending on benchmarks and integrations. The first week is mapping and smoke tests, second week is 24/7 benchmark run.
[08:38] Laura Kim: Anything special for data residency? We need EU-only for some flows.
[08:44] Jordan Liu: We support region pinning and Private deployments with EU-only control planes and data residency guarantees. We'll include region options in the proposal.
[08:55] Ethan Park: Ok wrapping up, quick recap: we'll send parity spreadsheet, security docs, and a benchmark template. Customer to share prompts and logs. We'll schedule a pilot kickoff next week.
[09:10] Samir Patel: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:15] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up by EOD with links and notes.
[09:22] [End of transcript]
notes: Transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts and speaker mislabels (Speaker 5), per usual Fireflies export. Shared artifacts: parity-spreadsheet link, security pack link, console optimize screenshot referenced.
